title: Growing winter squash and pumpkins
subtitle: Space-hungry climbers that cure into months of winter storage
excerpt: Winter squash and pumpkins are sown indoors in April, planted out in late May, and harvested in October when the skins have hardened. They need space, warmth, and a rich soil to produce well, but cured fruits store through the winter with no refrigeration needed.
sourceNotes: RHS squash growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. USDA cooperative extension notes on winter squash production, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: Leaving harvested squash and pumpkins in a warm place (ideally 27 to 30°C) for 10 to 14 days after picking to harden the skin and heal any surface wounds before storage. Cured squash stores better and longer than uncured; the skin toughens and the flesh becomes drier and sweeter. A warm greenhouse, porch, or windowsill in an Indian summer works well.

content.text: Winter squash and pumpkins are the same genus (Cucurbita maxima, C. moschata, C. pepo) and grown the same way. The difference is in the variety and end use: pumpkins for display and soup, Crown Prince and Butternut for long-storing dense-fleshed winter squash. Both need space: trailing varieties spread to 2 to 3 metres. Bush varieties are more compact but less productive.

Sow indoors from late April, one seed per 9 cm pot, on its side, 2.5 cm deep. Keep at 18 to 21°C. Germination takes 5 to 10 days. Squash grows fast once germinated; don't sow too early or the plant outgrows the pot before it can go out. Harden off carefully before planting out in late May.

Full sun, very rich, moisture-retentive soil. Plant on a mound of well-rotted manure or compost raised 15 cm above the surrounding soil to give warm, well-drained root conditions. Space trailing varieties 1.8 m apart; bush varieties 1.2 m apart. Plant out no earlier than late May; squash is frost-tender and check weather forecasts carefully.

Water deeply at the base twice a week in dry weather; avoid wetting the leaves. Feed every two weeks with a high-potash fertiliser once the first fruits have set. Trailing plants can be trained or left to sprawl; placing a tile or piece of wood under developing fruits prevents rot. In a short summer, limit each plant to two or three fruits and remove excess fruits while small to allow the remainder to develop fully.

Harvest in September or October before the first frost. The fruit is ready when the stem has corked and the skin sounds hollow when tapped. Cut with 5 cm of stalk attached; fruits without a stalk rot quickly.
for 10 to 14 days in a warm place before storage. Store in a cool, dry, frost-free place; properly cured winter squash keeps three to six months.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The main squash problems in UK growing.

items.symptom: Powdery white coating on leaves from midsummer
items.cause: Powdery mildew, common in squash from August onwards.
items.fix: Mildew is largely cosmetic and rarely affects fruits that have already set. Remove the worst affected leaves; maintain consistent watering at the roots.

items.symptom: Fruits rot at the base while still on the plant
items.cause: Direct soil contact in wet conditions.
items.fix: Place a tile, stone, or piece of cardboard under each developing fruit. Ensure good air circulation around the plants.
